Guneeth Palakurthy · Posted 5 months ago in General # Best Practices for Avoiding Adaptive Overfitting in Kaggle Competitions I am recently reading the Kaggle book and came across this beautiful set of best practices for competitive machine learning. In competitive machine learning, preventing adaptive overfitting is crucial for ensuring models generalize well to unseen data. Here are key strategies to improve model validation and robustness: ## **1. Build Strong Cross-Validation (CV) Systems** * Use **local validation** effectively to ensure models perform well beyond the leaderboard. * Avoid over-reliance on **public leaderboard feedback**, as repeated submissions may lead to leaderboard overfitting. Handle Non-i.i.d. Distributions** * When training and test sets have different distributions, standard validation may not work. * Identify distribution shifts by checking if specific validation splits yield consistently better results. Correlate Local Scores with the Public Leaderboard** * If **local validation scores** and **public leaderboard rankings** align, the model likely generalizes well. * If they don’t, it may indicate that the **public leaderboard does not reflect the private test distribution**. * Train a classifier to **differentiate between training and test data**. * If the classifier easily separates them, it signals a **distribution shift**, meaning the test set is not representative of the training data. * **Combine multiple models** using techniques like bagging, boosting, and stacking. * Ensembling helps reduce overfitting and improves generalization, especially for **small datasets** where single models may capture noise. By following these best practices, you can improve model reliability, avoid leaderboard overfitting, and enhance performance in Kaggle competitions. Title: Why the train/validate/test split helps to avoid overfitting — 04 | Analytics Vidhya
A model which over fits to the data is like a student who has just memorised all the answers to a set of past papers, but has learnt none of the underlying concepts. **Validation set** - this is the subset of the total data that will be used to test the models performance during training, typically 10% of the total data. **Test set** - this is the subset of the total data that will be used to test the final models performance, typically 20% of the total data. For our model, the train set is the data it uses to actually update its weights and biases to reduce the loss. For our model, we test its performance on the validation dataset after every epoch ( after every complete pass of the training dataset through the model ). If we see the validation loss increasing, we know we are now overfitting to the training data. For our model, this is the final data set we use to test its real world performance. **This dataset can only be used once.** If it turns out the models performance is inadequate we must go back through this entire process of training, validating and testing a new model. OK, so we can flag for over fitting by holding back part of our data and validating our model during training. The test set is used as the final data set to test our final trained models accuracy. Well, whats stopping us from just using the validation data set to test our final model as well? Imagine you are training a model to classify some digits from the MNIST data set. Now you train the model and after every epoch, test it on the test set. We still have yet to see whether the gains made on the validation loss are due to a superior model or due to our model being optimised on that data set. **But now we test on a new dataset.** This way we can be sure our models performance is genuinely improving and its not just becoming more optimised on a specific set of data.

# The Dark Side of Pretrained Models: Hidden Overfitting. Pretrained Models: Hidden Overfitting Threats. Pretrained models are the power tools of modern AI. Unlike traditional overfitting, which is easy to spot in training metrics, *hidden overfitting* stays buried—only revealing itself when your model encounters real-world data. Fine-tuned models often show continuous validation gains. When pretrained models are repurposed on small or domain-mismatched datasets, they may pick up noise or spurious correlations that don’t generalize beyond the test set. In one benchmark, ImageNet-pretrained models used for dermatology classification plateaued with a 6% validation overfitting gap, while self-supervised models generalized better (Matas et al., 2025). — A comprehensive review of transfer learning strategies, including overfitting risks and domain adaptation. (2019) found that small models trained from scratch outperformed pretrained networks in medical imaging because the latter failed to learn relevant clinical features (Raghu et al., 2019). Comparing visible and hidden overfitting through training and validation loss patterns over epochs."). But in transfer learning, loss may stay low even as the model overfits to hidden noise or shortcut signals. #### Are smaller models better for avoiding hidden overfitting? When working with niche data (e.g., legal, radiology, or aviation logs), consider **domain-adaptive pretraining**—further pretraining the model on in-domain unlabeled text before fine-tuning. #### Can hidden overfitting occur even with large, diverse training datasets? A model trained on millions of images may still overfit to artifact-rich data (like stock images) and fail on user-generated content. In A/B tests, if a new fine-tuned model performs well on 90% of segments but drops significantly on a niche user group or geographic region, it’s a strong indicator of hidden overfitting from training on unbalanced or misaligned data. Failing to spot hidden overfitting early leads to brittle models, wasted compute, and real-world failures.
